title: Check Without Asking
tag: One classroom move, under three minutes, for the teacher who teaches content, not English.

beats.say: Six Moves, from EL Publishing. Move five: check without asking do you understand.

chunks.text: Six Moves, from EL Publishing. Move five: check without asking do you understand.

beats.say: You finish explaining. You ask, does everyone understand? Everyone nods. The newcomer nods hardest, because nodding is the one thing they can do perfectly. You move on. Nobody understood.

chunks.text: You finish explaining. You ask, does everyone understand? Everyone nods.
The newcomer nods hardest, because nodding is the one thing they can do perfectly. You move on.
Nobody understood.

a: Yes is the polite answer in every language
It requires English to answer honestly
It checks one student at a time, or none
beats.say: Do you understand fails for three reasons. Yes is the polite answer in every language. Answering honestly requires English the student may not have. And it checks one student, or none — a nod from thirty people is no information at all.

beats.say: The move: check in a way that doesn't require English to answer, and that every student answers at once.

a: Point to it on the diagram
beats.say: Point to the nucleus on your diagram. Thirty fingers. You can see in two seconds who has it.

chunks.text: Point to the nucleus on your diagram. Thirty fingers. You can see in two seconds who has it.

beats.say: Is this a plant cell or an animal cell? One finger for plant, two for animal. Hold them up.

chunks.text: Is this a plant cell or an animal cell? One finger for plant, two for animal. Hold them up.

a: Sort the cards into two piles
beats.say: Sort these six cards into plant and animal. A level one can do it without a word.

chunks.text: Sort these six cards into plant and animal. A level one can do it without a word.

beats.say: Draw the process in three boxes. No sentences required.

chunks.text: Draw the process in three boxes. No sentences required.

a: Finish my sentence: “The nucleus controls the…”
beats.say: Finish my sentence. The nucleus controls the — and they say, cell. That's participation. It builds up.

chunks.text: Finish my sentence. The nucleus controls the — and they say, cell. That's participation. It builds up.

beats.say: Every one of those is answered by every student at the same moment, without a sentence of English, and you get a read on the whole room in ten seconds.

chunks.text: Every one of those is answered by every student at the same moment, without a sentence of English, and you get a read on the whole room in ten seconds.

a: Who can tell me what the nucleus does?
Thumbs up if the nucleus controls the cell. Thumbs sideways if it stores energy.
Does the nucleus control the cell, or store energy?
beats.say: And when you do ask a question out loud, make the question carry the words. Instead of what does the nucleus do, ask: does the nucleus control the cell, or store energy? Now the student has the words. They say, control the cell. Next week you ask the open question, and they've heard themselves say it before.

a: Half the room missed it: one more example, different channel
The newcomer missed it: partner shows, not translates
beats.say: Then do something with what you saw. If they have it, move on. If half the room missed it, one more example — in a different channel: a picture, a gesture, the board. If the newcomer missed it, their partner's job is to show them, not translate for them.
